confidence_note: Book text not read; facts from a strategy+business article, a PopMatters review and search summaries. Old-text figures (9 quintillion, 1971 2,300 transistors, 2020 50 billion, Indian legend, 32nd square as now) omitted as unsupported or post-dating the book.
facts: Rice story: one grain on the first of 64 squares, doubling each time; by the 32nd square about 4 billion grains, by the 64th more than 18 quintillion, a pile taller than Mount Everest; some versions have the inventor executed.

Ray Kurzweil's 'second half of the chessboard' (1999); the authors count from 1958 (first commercial silicon transistors) and say digital technology is in the second half, where numbers outstrip comprehension.
Moore 1965: transistor counts double regularly, later about every two years; an observation, not a physical law.
1982 Osborne Executive: 500 times larger, 100 times heavier, ten times more expensive, 1/100 as fast as a 2007 iPhone; 2011 iPad 2 matched the 1985 Cray-2 (inflation-adjusted $33 million).

DARPA 2002: US$1 million for a driverless race over 150 miles of Mojave Desert; 2004 no finisher, farthest 7.4 miles; under six years later Google's car had hundreds of thousands of accident-free miles.
Our brains are not equipped to grasp sustained exponential growth.
scene_details: one grain on the first square, doubling to 64
a pile taller than Mount Everest
tension: A tale of rice shows how doubling outruns intuition, and computing has been doubling since 1958.
opening_idea: Open on the 2004 desert race with no finisher, or on the rice.
